questions.text: In the Cox model h(t|X) = h₀(t)·exp(β₁X₁ + β₂X₂), if a covariate X₁ has estimated coefficient β̂₁ = −0.42, what is the hazard ratio for a one-unit increase in X₁?
questions.explanation: The hazard ratio for a one-unit increase in X₁ is HR = exp(β₁) = exp(−0.42) ≈ 0.66. This means patients with X₁ one unit higher have 34% lower instantaneous hazard. The coefficient β₁ is the log-hazard ratio; exp(β₁) converts it to the multiplicative hazard ratio scale.

questions.text: The Cox partial likelihood eliminates the baseline hazard h₀(t) from estimation, so β can be estimated without specifying the form of h₀(t).
questions.explanation: This is the key insight behind Cox's partial likelihood. At each event time t_i, the probability that patient i died (given that one death occurred among the risk set) involves the ratio exp(β⊤Xᵢ) / ∑_{j∈R(tᵢ)} exp(β⊤Xⱼ). The baseline hazard h₀(tᵢ) appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels, leaving a function of β only. This makes the Cox model semi-parametric.

questions.text: A Cox model for lung cancer includes sex (1=male, 2=female). The output shows: coef(sex) = −0.53, exp(coef) = 0.588, p = 0.002. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Female patients have a 53% lower hazard than males at every time point
After adjusting for other covariates, females have approximately 41% lower instantaneous risk of death than males at any given time
Female patients survive on average 0.588 days longer than males
The model is misspecified because the coefficient is negative
questions.explanation: exp(−0.53) ≈ 0.588, so the hazard ratio for female vs male is 0.588. This means females have about 1 − 0.588 = 41.2% lower hazard at every time point, after adjusting for the other covariates in the model. This is a conditional statement — it holds for patients with identical values of all other predictors. The p-value of 0.002 means this difference is statistically significant.

questions.text: The proportional hazards assumption states that the hazard ratio between two patients is:
options: Proportional to the event rate at each time point
Equal to 1 when covariates are mean-centred
Determined by the baseline hazard h₀(t)
questions.explanation: The PH assumption states that h(t|X)/h(t|X*) = exp(β⊤(X−X*)), which does not depend on t. The hazard ratio is constant over time — the two patients' hazard curves are parallel on the log scale. If a treatment works only for the first six months and then loses effect, the PH assumption is violated and the hazard ratio is time-varying.

questions.text: In R, cox.zph() tests the proportional hazards assumption by testing whether the scaled Schoenfeld residuals have a significant linear trend over time. A p-value below 0.05 suggests a violation.
questions.explanation: cox.zph() regresses scaled Schoenfeld residuals on a function of time (default: rank of event times). Under PH, the expected residuals should be flat — no trend. A significant slope (p < 0.05) suggests the effect of that covariate changes over time, violating PH. Remedies include stratification (strata() in the model formula), adding a time-by-covariate interaction, or switching to an AFT model.

questions.text: To predict the absolute survival probability S(t|X) for a new patient from a Cox model, you additionally need:
options: The Breslow estimator of the cumulative baseline hazard H₀(t) from basehaz()
The KM estimate of the marginal survival function
A parametric distribution for h₀(t) specified at model fitting time
questions.explanation: S(t|X) = exp(−H₀(t)·exp(β̂⊤X)). The Cox model only estimates β; the baseline cumulative hazard H₀(t) must be estimated separately. The Breslow estimator, available in R via basehaz(), provides a non-parametric step-function estimate of H₀(t). Absolute survival prediction therefore requires both the fitted coefficients and the Breslow baseline.
